newsitem.title: FRANCE: Sanofi seeks mergers to double size - source.
newsitem.headline: Sanofi seeks mergers to double size - source.

text.p: French pharmaceuticals company Sanofi is looking for one or two partners to allow it to double its size and meet development costs in the medium and long term, a source close to the company said on Tuesday.
Sanofi and Elf Aquitaine, which owns 55 percent of Sanofi, declined to comment.

Sanofi wants a 2.5 percent share of the world market and a market capitalisation of around 100 billion francs ($17.93 billion), while retaining control of strategy under chairman Jean-Francois Dehecq, the source said.
Any mergers could be done in two stages, with one in Europe and the second in the United States, said the source, who declined to be named.
Created 24 years ago, Sanofi currently ranks 23rd with a 1.5 percent world market share.
Elf has said it wants to cut its Sanofi holding to between 20 and 40 percent to allow Sanofi to find partners to speed up development and boost profitability.
Sanofi's current capitalisation is around 56 billion francs.
The source said the company's 1996 net profit should show an increase of nearly 10 percent after 1995 net profit of 1.58 billion francs, up 18.65 percent.
There are few firms which meet Sanofi's criteria. Besides size and independence, they include a complementary product portfolio in terms of maturity as well as geographical fit.
These considerations rule out a merger with Rhone-Poulenc, which would add nothing in geographic and product terms and would have a high social cost, the source said.
In New York, Rhone-Poulenc Rorer's chief financial officer Patrick Langlois told Reuters that his company's priorities were innovation and the launching of new products.
"Even if Sanofi is a good pharmaceuticals company, it might not be a perfect fit because of the geography of its business," he said.

The source said Sanofi's chairman believed a merger was all the more necessary in view of the marketing costs of new products and development of second-generation products which would weigh on future net profits.
He feared the share price, which rose nearly 50 percent last year, would reverse direction and leave Sanofi vulnerable to a takeover.
Dehecq's desire for an alliance as early as 1997 forced Elf chairman Philippe Jaffre to decide between the oil company's three activities -- oil, chemicals and pharmaceuticals.
A choice was needed as Elf's current development capacity did not allow it to meet its objective of being among the top 10 in each of the three sectors.
"A decision had to be made between chemicals and health, bearing in mind that chemicals and oil have price earnings ratio close to 15 times against 30 times for health," the source said.
Jaffre surprised the market by announcing on December 19 that he would not insist on keeping a majority in Sanofi.
The quality of discoveries in Africa which allowed Elf to revise upward the contribution from exploration may have influenced his decision, the source added.
($1=5.577 French Franc)
